answer.label: Not W. Edwards Deming — actually Paul Batalden, after Arthur Jones
answer.authorDates: Founding chair of the Institute for Healthcare Improvement · emeritus professor of pediatrics and health policy, Dartmouth
answer.sourceLine: Deming never wrote this sentence, and it appears nowhere in Wikiquote’s sourced Deming quotations ↗. By the account the Institute for Healthcare Improvement published on 21 August 2015 ↗, drawn from Paul Batalden and Earl Conway themselves, Batalden coined this “system” wording as a corollary to Arthur Jones’s line about organizations — Deming’s teaching shaped the thinking, but not this sentence.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Coined by Paul Batalden as a corollary for health professionals
“All organizations are perfectly designed to get the results they get!” — Arthur Jones (Procter & Gamble, UK)
David P. Hanna (Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1988), p. 36 — the page IHI cites
Susan Carr, “A Quotation with a Life of Its Own,” Patient Safety & Quality Healthcare, July/August 2008
Batalden and Conway’s own account, 2015 — PSQH blog, 3 August; republished by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement, 21 August

source.excerpt: “All organizations are perfectly designed to get the results they get!” — Arthur Jones, as David Hanna recorded him. And then the corollary, made for health professionals “less interested in ‘organizations’ than in ‘systems’”: “Every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets.”
trail: Summer 2006 — the saying is in print in health care and in Batalden’s mouth, with no mention of Deming: in Doug McInnis’s article “What System?”, Dartmouth Medicine reports that Batalden “is fond of the saying” ↗. The article names no originator at all.

July/August 2008 — the first explicit credit, and the first investigation of the drift: in Patient Safety & Quality Healthcare, editor Susan Carr calls the line “Dr. Paul Batalden’s observation” ↗ and runs a correction after IHI challenged a citation her magazine had printed crediting a 1984 book (Barry Clemson, Cybernetics: A New Management Tool). She finds it pinned in print on Berwick, on Deming, “occasionally, to Batalden,” and once on a David Beckwith, MD.

August 2015 — Batalden and Earl Conway publish the origin story themselves — on the PSQH blog on the 3rd, republished by IHI on the 21st: Batalden “created a corollary to the Jones words,” and Jones’s original ran “All organizations are perfectly designed to get the results they get!” Read the post ↗

2018 — the drift is still being acknowledged in the field: the Tower Foundation writes that the quote “is attributed to a range of people, including: Don Berwick, W. Edwards Deming, and Dr. Paul Batalden” ↗

Still absent from the record — no version of the line, and no quotation containing the words “perfectly designed,” appears on Wikiquote’s W. Edwards Deming page ↗, in its sourced sections or its misattributed one.
source.cutTag: Origin, in the participants’ own account
source.excerptNote: Both wordings are quoted as IHI gives them, from the accounts of Paul Batalden and Earl Conway; the Jones line, exclamation mark and all, is cited there to page 36 of Hanna’s book. Deming’s name appears in that account only as an influence on the two men.

source.rightsNote: There is no pre-1931 source for this line, so nothing here is public domain. The earliest printed form in the documented chain is Arthur Jones’s sentence in David P. Hanna’s Designing Organizations for High Performance (Addison-Wesley, 1988), and the “system” wording is Batalden’s later coinage — both modern and treated here as in copyright. Quoting a single aphorism with attribution is ordinary fair use; reproducing Hanna’s or Batalden’s surrounding text is not.

author.name: Paul Batalden
author.kicker: The true originator of this wording
author.heading: Who actually coined it
author.metaLine: American pediatrician and health-care quality-improvement leader · founding chair of the IHI board of directors
author.bio: Paul Batalden, MD, is a pediatrician by training who became one of the central figures in American health-care quality improvement: co-founder and founding chair of the board of the Institute for Healthcare Improvement, and an emeritus professor of pediatrics, community and family medicine, and health policy and clinical practice at Dartmouth’s Geisel School of Medicine. Earlier he served as assistant surgeon general and director of the Bureau of Community Health Services, and he later founded the U.S. VA National Quality Scholars program and IHI’s Health Professions Educational Collaborative. He was directly influenced by W. Edwards Deming’s thinking about systems and variation — which is exactly why the line he coined is so often handed back to Deming.

misattribution.heading: Four names, one sentence
misattribution.intro: This is a quotation with a documented chain of custody — and the famous name at the end of it is the one that did not say it.

items.why: Deming (1900–1993) is the name on nearly every graphic and slide, but the sentence is not in his work. Wikiquote’s Deming page ↗ contains no quotation with the words “perfectly designed” anywhere on it. What IHI records is influence, not authorship: Deming’s theory of variation shaped how both Earl Conway and Paul Batalden thought about systems ↗.

Because the line became house language in health-care improvement, IHI’s co-founder often gets it too. The Tower Foundation, writing on system redesign, notes plainly that “this quote is attributed to a range of people, including: Don Berwick, W. Edwards Deming, and Dr. Paul Batalden” ↗.

IHI’s account is explicit: “Paul created a corollary to the Jones words: ‘Every system is perfectly designed to get the results it gets’ and has shared the words with many others” — the switch from organizations to systems made for health professionals. Read IHI’s account ↗.

Jones, a Procter & Gamble colleague of David Hanna’s, is quoted saying “All organizations are perfectly designed to get the results they get!” — recorded by Hanna, per IHI, on page 36 of Designing Organizations for High Performance (Addison-Wesley, 1988) ↗. Earl Conway, who knew and worked with Hanna at P&G, brought the insight to the US Quality Council of the Conference Board, which he and Batalden co-chaired in the 1970s.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is Deming-shaped; the sentence is Batalden’s, built on Arthur Jones’s — on the testimony of the two men who were there ↗.

context.heading: Why this line travels — and why it lands on Deming
lead: It is the sentence people reach for when they want to say that a bad outcome was produced rather than merely suffered: not bad luck, not bad apples, but a system doing exactly what its design makes it do. That framing took hold first in health care. In the Summer 2006 issue of Dartmouth Medicine, Batalden is described as “fond of the saying” and glossing it himself: “If we keep doing what we have been doing, we’ll keep getting what we’ve always gotten” ↗ — an argument for redesign over tinkering.

The reason Deming’s name sticks to it is that the thought really is Deming-shaped. IHI’s account notes that Deming’s theory of variation and his insistence on redesigning systems influenced both Earl Conway and Batalden, and Wikiquote’s sourced section does carry Deming’s genuine definition from The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education (1993): “A system is a network of interdependent components that work together to try to accomplish the aim of the system” ↗. A line that sounds like a compression of that idea gets filed under its most famous exponent — which is how attribution usually goes wrong.
context.detailsSummary: Variant wordings, and what the drift tells you
detailsBody: Several forms circulate under Deming’s name — “…to get the result that it does,” “…to get the results that it gets” — and the unstable wording is itself evidence. Lines copied from a printed page tend to hold their shape; lines passed along in talks and slide decks drift, and this one drifted.

The other tell is the chain of credit. Arthur Jones said it of organizations; Batalden restated it for systems because, as IHI puts it, some health professionals were “less interested in ‘organizations’ than in ‘systems.’” Each retelling swapped a word and shed a name, until the last name standing was the most famous one in the room.
context.pull: “If we keep doing what we have been doing, we’ll keep getting what we’ve always gotten.” — Paul Batalden, quoted in Dartmouth Medicine, Summer 2006
